raw_text:
The objective of this research is to investigate and understand the reasons behind the persistent completion-time differences observed in sites employing the same nominal work process. The scope of the research encompasses identifying measurable factors that account for these differences and distinguishing between competing explanations through empirical observations.

Assumptions
    - Work processes are documented and similar across the sites.
    - Completion times are consistently recorded.
    - Variability in completion times is significant enough to warrant investigation.
    - Differences in measurable factors can influence completion times.

Research design
    This study will employ a mixed-methods design, combining Quantitative and Qualitative methodologies. Quantitatively, a comparative analysis of measurable factors will be conducted using regression analysis to identify predictors of completion times. Qualitatively, ethnographic observations will be performed to gather in-depth insights into how the work process is applied and any deviations or additional practices that may influence completion times.

Data or evidence needed
    - Baseline completion time data collected from each site.
    - Detailed descriptions of the nominal work process for each site.
    - Observations of work practices in action.
    - Interviews with key stakeholders (managers, workers) to gather qualitative insights.

Measurement
    - Completion time for each task or job at each site.
    - Measurable factors such as workload, resource availability, employee skills, and work environment quality.
    - Observational scores capturing deviations from the nominal work process and additional practices observed.

Analysis
    Quantitative data will be analyzed using regression analysis to determine which measurable factors significantly predict completion time. Qualitative data will be thematically analyzed to identify recurring themes and patterns that may explain the observed differences in completion times.

Decision / stopping rule
    The research will end when we have identified and statistically validated the significant predictors of completion time, or when data saturation is reached in the qualitative phase, indicating that no new insights can be obtained from additional observations.

Limitations
    - The study may not capture all subtle or unobservable factors influencing completion times.
    - Self-report bias could affect the qualitative data collected from interviews.
    - Variability in site-specific contexts, such as cultural influences or past organizational events, may not be fully accounted for in the quantitative analysis.
    - The generalizability of findings might be limited due to the sample selected. Future studies could expand the scope to more diverse sites to assess robustness.
